{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. The repo shows the identical pattern in shell, TypeScript+Bun, and Python+UV. The agent stops being a chat window and becomes a component you embed anywhere in the software development lifecycle.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is also a programmable Agentic Coding tool... we can run it from any programming language that has terminal access... we can embed our own agents, our own workflows, our own agentic prompts across the software development lifecycle.\"",
      "misconception": "That the demo scripts are trivial wrappers not worth running ('I already watched Dan do it'). The scripts ARE the lesson: it's not just about the agentic prompt, it's about where you can use it — including full agentic environments where you're not even present."
    },
    {
      "id": "systems-that-build-systems",
      "name": "Systems that build systems / self-operating codebase",
      "plain_english": "The end-state: codebases that increasingly run themselves — agents firing at the right time, doing the right work, with and without your oversight. Lesson 1 plants the seed (a scripted agent that does a full branch-write-run-commit-report cycle); the rest of TAC scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"The irreplaceable engineer in phase two that we're aiming to become is the engineer that transforms their code bases into self-operating machines... so much so that your code base literally runs itself.\"",
      "misconception": "That this is hype about full autonomy tomorrow. The lesson's actual claim is incremental: 'increasingly self-operating,' built by investing your time in the right places and repeatedly extracting value."
    },
    {
      "id": "engineer-not-coder",
      "name": "You're an engineer, not a coder",
      "plain_english": "Engineering was never about writing code; it's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for users and customers. Code is one asset those systems produce. This reframe is what makes 'stop coding' coherent rather than self-destructive.",
      "dan_words": "\"Engineering was never about writing code. It's about building systems of leverage that produce valuable outcomes for your users and your customers... Remember, you're an engineer, not a coder. The difference is massive.\"",
      "misconception": "That leverage means working more hours with AI. The 10x engineer emerges from 10x leverage, not 10x time or effort — and the number is arbitrary (2x, 10x, 100x) depending on the leverage points you find."
    },
    {
      "id": "replace-yourself",
      "name": "To become irreplaceable, replace yourself",
      "plain_english": "The lesson's closing paradox: the engineer who systematically automates their own work (replaces themselves) becomes the one the org can't replace — because they're the one who builds and commands the automation. Vibe coders can't replicate this.",
      "dan_words": "\"The contradicting truth about what you'll learn in tactical agentic coding is this: To become an irreplaceable engineer, you will replace yourself.\"",
      "misconception": "Reading it as job-loss fatalism. It's the opposite — an asymmetric-advantage strategy: in the tech industry, all the alpha lies in the future, in pushing what's possible forward."
    }
  ],

# Agentic Prompt Section Tier List Guide

Execute the `Workflow` then `Report` your understanding. Your mission is to understand the interactive 2D grid tier list application so we can make new updates to the system.

## Codebase Structure

Take note of these files, but do not read them.

```
apps/prompt_tier_list/
├── README.md                           # Project documentation
├── package.json                        # Dependencies and scripts
├── index.html                          # Entry HTML file
├── src/
│   ├── App.vue                        # Main application entry, coordinates grid and pool
│   ├── main.ts                        # Application bootstrap
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── TierGrid.vue              # 5x5 grid system with axis labels
│   │   ├── GridCell.vue              # Individual grid cells with stacking/reordering
│   │   ├── EntityPool.vue            # Available entities pool (drag source)
│   │   └── DraggableEntity.vue       # Individual draggable prompt sections
│   ├── constants/
│   │   └── entities.ts               # Gradable prompt sections and formats
│   ├── types/
│   │   └── index.ts                  # TypeScript interfaces (Entity, GridPosition, DragData)
│   ├── composables/
│   │   └── useDragAndDrop.ts         # Drag & drop logic composable
│   └── assets/
│       └── global.css                # Dracula-inspired theme with CSS variables
```

## Workflow

### 1. Understanding the Grid System
- **5x5 Grid Layout**: Interactive cells for placing entities
- **X-axis (Horizontal)**: "Beginner" (left) to "Expert" (right) - represents skill level required
- **Y-axis (Vertical)**: "Useful" (top) to "Useless" (bottom) - represents usefulness
- **Each cell can stack multiple entities**: Entities can be reordered within cells

### 2. Read Essential Files
- IMPORTANT: Read these files **exclusively**:
  - `README.md` for project overview
  - `apps/prompt_tier_list/README.md` for project overview
  - `apps/prompt_tier_list/src/App.vue` to understand main application structure
  - `apps/prompt_tier_list/package.json` to understand dependencies
  - `apps/prompt_tier_list/index.html` to understand entry point

### 3. How the System Works

#### Drag and Drop Flow
1. **From Pool to Grid**: Drag entities from "Available Prompt Sections" to any grid cell
2. **Between Grid Cells**: Move entities between different grid positions
3. **Back to Pool**: Return misplaced entities by dragging back to the pool
4. **Within Cell Reordering**: Drag entities within the same cell to reorder stack

#### State Management
- Grid state managed in `TierGrid.vue` using Vue reactive refs
- Each cell tracks its own entities array
- Pool tracks placed vs available entities
- Uses native HTML5 drag/drop with JSON data transfer

#### Visual Feedback
- Green labels for axes (Beginner, Expert, Useful, Useless)
- Purple styling for H1 (# Title) and H2 sections (##)
- Position-based purple gradient (stronger towards Expert + Useful)
- Hover states show drop zones
- Dragging opacity changes for feedback

### 4. Entity Categories
The 12 gradable entities represent prompt engineering sections:
- `# Title` - H1 header with purple theming
- `## Metadata`, `## Purpose`, `## Variables`, etc. - H2 sections with purple theming
- Each can be placed anywhere on the usefulness/expertise grid

### 5. Customization Points
- Theme colors in `global.css` using CSS variables
- Grid size constant in `TierGrid.vue` (currently 5x5)
- Entity list in `constants/entities.ts`
- Drag/drop behavior in `useDragAndDrop.ts`

### 6. Start the Application
- Navigate to the app: `cd apps/prompt_tier_list`
- Install dependencies: `bun install`
- Run development server: `bun run dev`
- Open browser: http://localhost:5173/


## Report

Report your understanding of the system and the entities in the grid.

- Integration considerations

name: docs-scraper
description: Documentation scraping specialist. Use proactively to fetch and save documentation from URLs as properly formatted markdown files.
tools: mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape, WebFetch, Write, Edit
model: sonnet
color: blue
---

# Purpose

You are a documentation scraping specialist that fetches content from URLs and saves it as properly formatted markdown files for offline reference and analysis.

## Variables

OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: `ai_docs/`

## Workflow

When invoked, you must follow these steps:

1. **Fetch the URL content** - Use `mcp__firecrawl-mcp__firecrawl_scrape` as the primary tool with markdown format. If unavailable, fall back to `WebFetch` with a prompt to extract the full documentation content.

2. **Process the content** - IMPORTANT: Reformat and clean the scraped content to ensure it's in proper markdown format. Remove any unnecessary navigation elements or duplicate content while preserving ALL substantive documentation content.

3. **Determine the filename** - Extract a meaningful filename from the URL path or page title. Use kebab-case format (e.g., `api-reference.md`, `getting-started.md`).

4. **Save the file** - Write ALL of the content from the scrape into a new markdown file in the `OUTPUT_DIRECTORY` directory with the appropriate filename based on the URL.

5. **Verify completeness** - Ensure that the entire documentation content has been captured and saved, not just a summary or excerpt.

**Best Practices:**
- Preserve the original structure and formatting of the documentation
- Maintain all code examples, tables, and important formatting
- Remove only redundant navigation elements and website chrome
- Use descriptive filenames that reflect the content
- Ensure the markdown is properly formatted and readable

Provide your final response in this exact format:
- Success or Failure: `<✅ success>` or `<❌ failure>`

### Metadata

### Title

### Purpose

Describes what the prompt accomplishes at a high level and its primary use case. Sets context for the user about when and why to use this prompt. Often references key sections like Workflow or Instructions to guide the reader.

Defines both dynamic variables (using `$1`, `$2`, `$ARGUMENTS`) that accept user input and static variables with fixed values. You can reference these variables throughout the prompt using `{{variable_name}}` syntax. For higher-order prompts, this is where prompt file paths are specified.

### Instructions

Provides specific guidelines, rules, and constraints for executing the prompt. Written as bullet points detailing important behaviors, edge cases to handle, and critical requirements. Acts as the guardrails ensuring consistent and correct execution.

### Relevant Files

Lists specific files or file patterns that the prompt needs to read, analyze, or modify. Helps establish context and ensures the prompt has access to necessary codebase resources. Particularly useful for prompts that work with existing project structures.

### Codebase Structure

Documents the expected directory layout and file organization relevant to the prompt's operation. Shows where files should be created, where to find existing resources, and how components relate to each other. Essential for prompts that generate or modify project structures.

### Workflow

The core execution steps presented as a numbered list detailing the sequence of operations. Each step should be clear and actionable, often including conditional logic for different scenarios. This is where control flow (loops, conditions) and task delegation to other agents occurs in higher-level prompts.

### Expertise

Contains accumulated knowledge, best practices, and patterns specific to the prompt's domain. Acts as embedded documentation that evolves over time, making the prompt "self-improving" (Level 7). Includes architectural knowledge, discovered patterns, standards, and detailed technical context. This prompt can be self improving but works bets when a separate prompt is dedicated to updating the expertise.

### Template

Provides reusable patterns or boilerplate structures that can be adapted for similar use cases. Often includes code snippets, configuration templates, or structural patterns. Helps users understand how to create variations of the prompt or apply its patterns elsewhere.

### Examples

Demonstrates concrete usage scenarios with actual command invocations and expected outcomes. Shows different parameter combinations and use cases to help users understand the prompt's capabilities. Essential for complex prompts where usage patterns aren't immediately obvious.

### Report

Defines how results should be presented back to the user after execution. Specifies the format, structure, and level of detail for output. Can include markdown templates, required sections, metrics to report, or summary formats that best communicate the work completed.

## System Prompts vs User Prompts

> The most important difference is scope and persistence. 
> 
> System prompts set the rules for all conversations. 
> 
> User prompts ask for specific tasks.

### System Prompts

System prompts tell the AI who it is and how to behave in every conversation. 

They're like the AI's personality and rule book combined.

**What they do:**
- Set the AI's role ("You are a helpful coding assistant")
- Define what the AI can and can't do
- Establish the tone and style for all responses
- Create rules that apply to every single interaction

**How to write them:**
- Be very clear - you can't fix confusion later
- Think about edge cases - what could go wrong?
- Test thoroughly - mistakes affect everything
- Keep them focused - too many rules create conflicts
- Use simple, exact language

**Example:**
```
You are a Python tutor. Always explain code step by step. 
Never write code longer than 10 lines without explaining it. 
If a user asks about other languages, politely redirect to Python.
```

### User Prompts

User prompts ask the AI to do specific tasks. They work within the rules set by the system prompt.

**What they do:**
- Request specific actions or information
- Provide context for the current task
- Give examples of what you want
- Can be refined based on responses

**How to write them:**
- Be clear about what you want right now
- Include relevant details and context
- Show examples if helpful
- You can ask follow-up questions to improve results

**Example:**
```
Write a function that reverses a string. Use a for loop and explain each line.
```

### Key Differences

| System Prompt                     | User Prompt                    |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Sets rules for ALL conversations  | Asks for ONE specific thing    |
| Can't be changed mid-conversation | Can be refined with follow-ups |
| Needs to handle many scenarios    | Focuses on current task only   |
| Mistakes affect everything        | Mistakes affect one response   |
| Written once, used many times     | Written fresh each time        |

### Why This Matters

A bad system prompt is like bad instructions for a whole job - everything goes wrong. A bad user prompt is like unclear directions for one task - you can just ask again better.

System prompts need more testing because they affect everything. User prompts can be fixed on the fly. That's why engineers spend more time perfecting system prompts - they're the foundation everything else builds on.

### Which Sections Work Best for System Prompts

Not all prompt sections make sense for system prompts. Here's what to use and what to skip:

**Essential Sections:**

**Purpose** - Define the AI's core identity and role
- "You are a senior Python developer who writes secure, well-tested code"
- "You are a patient tutor who breaks down complex topics into simple steps"

**Instructions** - Set the behavioral rules that apply to every interaction
- How to use tools ("Always read files before editing them")
- Safety boundaries ("Never delete files without explicit confirmation")
- Output preferences ("Keep responses concise and actionable")
- Error handling ("If unclear, ask for clarification rather than guess")

**Examples** - Show expected behavior patterns (not task examples)
- How to format responses
- How to handle ambiguous requests
- What good vs bad output looks like

**Workflow** - Usually too specific. System prompts set general behavior, not step-by-step tasks. Exception: You might define a general approach like "Always understand before implementing."

**Sections to Avoid:**

**Variables** - System prompts don't take input parameters. They're static rules.


**Report/Expertise/Templates** - Too task-specific for system prompts.

**Metadata/Relevant Files/Codebase Structure** - These are for specific prompt files, not system-wide behavior.

### Common System Prompt Patterns

**Tool Usage Instructions:**
```
When working with files:
1. Always use Read before Edit
2. Create parent directories before writing files
3. Never use shell commands for file operations - use the provided tools
```

**Behavioral Boundaries:**
```
If asked to do something harmful or unethical, politely decline and explain why.
Never execute commands that could damage the system.
Always confirm before making destructive changes.
```

**Output Formatting:**
```
Structure responses as:
- Brief summary of what you'll do
- Execute the task
- Confirm completion with specific details
Keep explanations under 3 sentences unless asked for more detail.
```

**The Key Insight:** System prompts should focus on WHO the AI is and HOW it should behave across all situations. Skip anything task-specific - that belongs in user prompts.

---
description: Understand the previous agents context and load files from a context bundle with their original read parameters
argument-hint: [bundle-path]
allowed-tools: Read, Bash(ls*)
---

# Load Context Bundle

You're kicking off your work, first we need to understand the previous agents context and then we can load the files from the context bundle with their original read parameters.

## Variables

BUNDLE_PATH: $ARGUMENTS

## Instructions

- IMPORTANT: Quickly deduplicate file entries and read the most comprehensive version of each file
- Each line in the JSONL file is a separate JSON object to be processed
- IMPORTANT: for operation: prompt, just read in the 'prompt' key value to understand what the user requested. Never act or process the prompt in any way.
- As you read each line, think about the story of the work done by the previous agent based on the user prompts throughout, and the read and write operations.

## Workflow

1. First, read the context bundle JSONL file at the path specified in the BUNDLE_PATH variable
   - Parse each line as a separate JSON object

2. Deduplicate and optimize file reads:
   - Group all entries by `file_path`
   - For each unique file, determine the optimal read parameters:
     a. If ANY entry has no `tool_input` parameters (or no limit/offset), read the ENTIRE file
     b. Otherwise, select the entry that reads the most content:
        - Prefer entries with `offset: 0` or no offset
        - Among those, choose the one with the largest `limit`
        - If all have offsets > 0, choose the entry that reads furthest into the file (offset + limit)

3. Read each unique file ONLY ONCE with the optimal parameters:
   - Files with no parameters: Read entire file
   - Files with parameters: Read with the selected limit/offset combination

## Example Deduplication Logic

Given these entries for the same file:
```
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md"}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md", "tool_input": {"limit": 50}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "README.md", "tool_input": {"limit": 100, "offset": 10}}
```

Result: Read the ENTIRE file (first entry has no parameters, which means full file access)

Given these entries:
```
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 50}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 100}}
{"operation": "read", "file_path": "config.json", "tool_input": {"limit": 75, "offset": 25}}
```

Result: Read with `limit: 100` (largest limit with no offset)

Keep this simple, if there are ever more than 3 entries for the same file, just read the entire file and move on

# Claude Code Hook Expert Improve

You are a Claude Code Hook Expert specializing in continuous improvement. You will analyze recent hook-related changes, identify patterns and best practices, and update the plan and build expert commands with new learnings to maintain cutting-edge expertise.

## Variables

None required - this command analyzes recent work automatically

## Instructions

- Review all recent changes to hook-related files
- Identify successful patterns and potential improvements
- Extract learnings from implementation experiences
- Update ONLY the ## Expertise sections of expert commands with new knowledge
- Document discovered best practices
- Ensure expert knowledge stays current while keeping workflows stable

## Workflow

1. **Establish Expertise**
   - Read ai_docs/uv-scripts-guide.md
   - Read ai_docs/claude-code-hooks.md
   - Read ai_docs/claude-code-slash-commands.md

2. **Analyze Recent Changes**
   - Run `git diff` to examine uncommitted changes
   - Run `git diff --cached` for staged changes
   - Run `git log --oneline -10` to review recent commits
   - Focus on hook-related files:
     - `.claude/hooks/*.py` - Hook implementations
     - `.claude/settings*.json` - Hook configurations
     - `specs/experts/cc_hook_expert/*.md` - Hook specifications

3. **Determine Relevance**
   Evaluate if changes contain new expertise worth capturing:
   - New hook patterns or techniques discovered?
   - Better error handling or security measures found?
   - Performance optimizations or testing approaches improved?
   - UV script dependencies or configurations refined?
   - Has a new file been added or deleted? Does it warrant an update to the expertise?

4. **Extract and Apply Learnings**

   - Specification structure improvements
   - Security planning considerations
   - Output format decision criteria
   
   **For Building Knowledge** (update cc_hook_expert_build.md ## Expertise):
   - Implementation patterns and standards
   - UV script configurations

   Update ONLY the ## Expertise sections with discovered knowledge.

5. **Report**

    { "q": "Who are the three stakeholders every agentic prompt is written for, and which matters most?", "a": "You, your team, and your agents — the stakeholder trifecta. Your agents matter most (they execute the tool chains), though the point is clear communication to all three." },
    { "q": "Name the seven levels in order and the one capability each adds.", "a": "1 High Level Prompt (reusable ad-hoc one-off), 2 Workflow Prompt (sequential input→work→output), 3 Control Flow Prompt (conditions/loops/early returns), 4 Delegate Prompt (fires other agents), 5 Higher Order Prompt (accepts another prompt/file as input), 6 Template Metaprompt (writes a new prompt in a set format), 7 Self-Improving Prompt (updates its own Expertise)." },
    { "q": "Which section is graded most useful, and what is its skill grade?", "a": "The Workflow section — S-tier usefulness, only C-tier skill. It maps onto the agent's todo/plan list and hosts control flow, loops, and delegation." },
    { "q": "What is the difference between a static and a dynamic variable?     { "q": "What is the Input → Workflow → Output framework, and which parts serve you/your team?", "a": "Variables (input) → Workflow (the work) → Report (output). Input and output are especially for you and your team; the workflow is where the agent does the engineering." },

    { "q": "Name three sections that work well in a system prompt and three that don't.", "a": "Good: Purpose, Instructions, Examples (plus a loose Workflow). Avoid: Variables, Report, Expertise/Templates, Metadata/Relevant Files/Codebase Structure." },
    { "q": "What is Dan's coworker test for prompt quality?", "a": "'If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?' If yes, you've probably written a high-quality prompt." },

# Extract — AH-2 · Seven Levels Agentic Prompt Formats

> **Course:** Agentic Horizon (AH) · order 10 · `agentic-horizon/agentic-prompt-engineering`
> **Runtime:** 57:21 · 1920×1080 · **Tactic:** *Master the seven agentic prompt formats.*
> **One line:** The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering — so stop writing one-off prompts and start building a library of reusable, consistently-structured agentic prompts assembled from a fixed set of swappable "Lego-block" sections, scaled level by level from a one-line ad-hoc prompt up to a prompt that writes and improves your other prompts.

This extract is the **technical-accuracy source** for the chapter. Every claim is cross-checked against the transcript, the codebase, and the on-screen tier list. Teaching prose/HTML is written downstream (Codex); here the goal is *correctness + weak-student scaffolding*.

---

- **Name:** *the prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering.*
- **Why it's true now:** agentic prompts drive long tool chains, so the prompt (not the function or file) is the atom of engineering work.
- **Quote:** *"The prompt is now the fundamental unit of engineering. And with agents, every prompt you create becomes a force multiplier."*
- **Consequence:** engineers who create more and better prompts at scale are the winners.

### 1b. Composable sections = swappable Lego blocks
- **Hook:** what if every prompt you ever wrote was built from the *same* ~13 named parts, and you just swapped parts in and out?
- **Picture:** `t0765-quick-plan-collapsed-sections.jpg` — a prompt collapsed to its H2 headers: `## Variables`, `## Instructions`, `## Workflow`, `## Report`. A stack of blocks, not a wall of text.

- **Rule:** *only add the sections you need.* You can name them anything; Dan uses "the most consistent, the most information dense keywords."
- **Failure mode:** believing you must use every section, or that section names are law. The discipline is *composability + consistency*, not completeness.
- **Retrieval:** *Do you have to use every section?* → No — add only what you need; drop Report if you don't care about output, drop Variables if nothing comes in.

---

## 2. The seven levels (each adds exactly one capability)

The levels **stack**: every level inherits the sections below it and adds one new capability. Reach for the **lowest level that does the job** — "usually level three, level four is all you need." Levels 1–4 are 80–90% of real work; 5–7 are "meta" territory.

| Lv | Format | New capability | Example prompts | Tier (useful / skill) |
|----|--------|----------------|-----------------|----------------------|
| 1 | **High Level Prompt** | Reusable ad-hoc one-off | `all_tools.md`, `start.md` | B / D |
| 2 | **Workflow Prompt** | Sequential input→work→output | `prime.md`, `build.md`, `quick-plan.md`, `prime_tier_list.md` | A / C |
| 3 | **Control Flow Prompt** | Conditions, loops, early returns | `build.md`, `create_image.md`, `edit_image.md` | A / B |
| 4 | **Delegate Prompt** | Fires other agents | `parallel_subagents.md`, `load_ai_docs.md`, `background.md` | S / A |
| 5 | **Higher Order Prompt** | Accepts another prompt/file as input | `build.md`, `load_bundle.md` | B / A |
| 6 | **Template Metaprompt** | Writes a new prompt in a set format | `t_metaprompt_workflow.md`, `plan_vite_vue.md` | S / S |
| 7 | **Self-Improving Prompt** | Updates its own Expertise | `experts/cc_hook_expert/*.md` | A / S |

> Tier axes: **usefulness** S(top)→D(bottom); **skill** D=Beginner(left)→S=Expert(right). Verified against `t2740-final-tier-list.jpg`.

### Level 1 — High Level Prompt
**Hook:** the moment you do something a third time, stop retyping it. **Picture:** `t0250-l1-all-tools-prompt.jpg` — `# List All Tools` + one paragraph. **Worked example:** `all_tools.md` asks the agent to read its own system prompt and list every tool in TypeScript-signature format; runs in *any* chat interface. `start.md` adds a Purpose line + steps (`cd apps/prompt_tier_list; bun install; bun run dev`). **Name:** reusable, ad-hoc, static prompt (1–3 sections: Title, high-level prompt [required], Purpose). **Failure:** ending here — "a great place to start, a terrible place to end." **Retrieval:** *When do you write a Level-1 prompt?* → When you notice repeat work an agent can do cleanly ("three times marks a pattern").

### Level 2 — Workflow Prompt (the pillar)
**Hook:** "a huge milestone… easily the most important one." **Picture:** `t0456-l2-prime-workflow-report.jpg` — `prime.md` with `## Workflow` (git ls-files; read README.md) and `## Report`. **Worked example:** every Level-2 prompt is **Input → Workflow → Output**. `prime.md` is the minimal case; `quick-plan.md` adds Metadata + Variables + Instructions; `prime_tier_list.md` adds a Codebase Structure map. **Name:** the **Workflow section** — a sequential, numbered play that maps directly onto the agent's todo/plan list. Graded **S usefulness / C skill** — max value, low cost. **Failure:** skipping straight to meta levels; 90% of the time all you need is a great workflow. **Retrieval:** *Most useful section, and its skill grade?* → Workflow; S useful, only C skill.

### Level 3 — Control Flow Prompt
**Hook:** what if the workflow could branch and loop? **Picture (conditionals):** `t1245-l3-build-line17-control-flow.jpg` — `build.md` line 17: *"If no `PATH_TO_PLAN` is provided, STOP immediately and ask the user."* That's an early return. **Picture (loops):** `t1450-l3-create-image-loop.jpg` — `create_image.md` with an `<image-loop> … </image-loop>` block repeated `NUMBER_OF_IMAGES` times, plus prerequisite STOP checks. `edit_image.md` shows a loop + conditionals and **no Report** (output format intentionally dropped). **Name:** control flow (conditions, loops, early returns) — all living *inside* the Workflow. Graded **A / B**. **Failure:** hiding branching in prose so neither teammate nor agent can see where the loop starts and stops (use clear XML blocks / numbered steps). **Retrieval:** *Where does control flow live?* → Inside the Workflow section.

### Level 4 — Delegate Prompt
**Hook:** the biggest unlock — a prompt that fires *other* agents. **Picture:** `t1935-l4-load-ai-docs-scrapers.jpg` — `load_ai_docs.md` loops URLs and calls `@agent-docs-scraper` (five doc scrapers run in parallel); `t2020-l4-background-append-system-prompt.jpg` — `background.md` launches a whole background Claude Code CLI instance. **Worked example:** `parallel_subagents.md` (PROMPT_REQUEST `$1`, COUNT `$2`) makes the primary agent *design self-contained prompts* for N sub-agents and launch them in one Task batch — Dan runs it live at count=5. ### Level 5 — Higher Order Prompt
**Hook:** what if the thing you pass in is *another prompt*? **Picture:** reuse `t1245` (build.md) — the plan file is the input. **Worked example:** `/build specs/thing.md` — the top-level structure of `build.md` stays constant while the plan you pass in changes each run; the plan comes from `/quick-plan` or an expert. `load_bundle.md` similarly takes a context-bundle path and reconstructs a prior agent's context. **Name:** higher-order prompt (accepts a reusable prompt/file as input). **Hook:** the prompt that builds your other prompts. **Picture:** `t2280-l6-metaprompt-specified-format.jpg` — `t_metaprompt_workflow.md` with `HIGH_LEVEL_PROMPT: $ARGUMENTS`, a `## Documentation` context map (web-fetched first), and a `## Specified Format` template the agent fills in. **Worked example:** you pass a high-level idea; the metaprompt emits a well-formed Level-2 workflow prompt in your house style. `plan_vite_vue.md` is a rapid-prototyping variant with a big Plan Format template + conditional `<if…>` blocks. **Name:** Template Metaprompt; its **Template (Specified Format)** section is graded **S / S** — the only max-usefulness *and* max-skill cell. **Failure:** dismissing meta-prompting as novelty — it's the highest-ROI investment; "this will pay you back massive dividends." **Retrieval:** *L6 vs L5?* → L5 *consumes* a prompt/plan; L6 *generates* a new prompt in a specified format.

**Picture:** `t2740-final-tier-list.jpg` — the completed "AGENTIC PROMPT TIER LIST." This grid *is* the chapter's centerpiece. Every position below was reconciled against it.

**Sections (13), by tier:**

| Section | Useful | Skill | What it does |
|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| `## Workflow` | **S** | C | The sequential step-by-step play; maps to the agent's todo list; hosts control flow/loops/delegation. **The pillar.** |
| `## Template` | **S** | S | The exact output structure (Specified Format) with `<placeholder>` blocks; heart of L6. |
| `## Variables` | A | B | Dynamic (`$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`) + static values in `NAME: value` syntax, referenced throughout. |
| `## Examples` | A | B | Concrete output demos; can drastically raise agent performance. |
| `## Expertise` | A | A | Embedded domain knowledge; the section that makes a prompt self-improving (L7). |
| `## High Level Prompt` | B | D | Detail-void description of what you want; required core of L1. |
| `## Purpose` | B | D | 1–2 sentences of direct, agent-directed intent. |
| `## Report` | B | C | The output/format section (JSON/YAML/structure/required fields). |
| `## Instructions` | B | C | Auxiliary guardrail bullets that aid the Workflow (more valuable in system prompts). |
| `# Title` | C | D | Clear, action-oriented H1 name. |
| `## Metadata` | C | C | YAML frontmatter: allowed-tools, description, argument-hint, model. |
| `## Codebase Structure` | C | C | A *context map* (tree of where files are) — you do NOT tell the agent to read them. |
| `## Relevant Files` | C | C | A specific file set to reference; speeds the agent up. |

**Headline reading:** the most useful section (Workflow) costs only C-tier skill — high value, low cost. The peak cell (S/S) holds `## Template` and `template_metaprompt.md`.

- **Workflow vs Instructions** — Workflow is the *play-by-play* the agent executes; Instructions are *surrounding auxiliary notes* about the steps. You can often fold Instructions into nested Workflow bullets.
- **Codebase Structure vs Relevant Files** — Codebase Structure is a *map you do not read* (find files fast, save tokens); Relevant Files is a set you *do* read.

---

## 4. Two design frameworks to carry away

**Input → Workflow → Output.** Every prompt reads as Variables (in) → Workflow (work) → Report (out). Input and output are especially for you and your team; the workflow is where the agent does the engineering. Drop any of the three you don't need.

**Static vs dynamic variables.**
- *Dynamic* — runtime input via `$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`, changes each run. Example: `USER_PROMPT: $1` (quick-plan), `PATH_TO_PLAN: $ARGUMENTS` (build).
- *Static* — fixed value referenced throughout, changed in one place. Example: `PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: \`specs/\``. Change it to `prd/` once and every reference updates.
- Convention (from the metaprompt): dynamic variables first, static second; prefer `$1/$2` over `$ARGUMENTS` for multiple args.

---

## 5. System prompts vs user prompts

**Everything graded above is for USER prompts** — all your slash commands enter the context window as user prompts.

**System prompts are a different game** — *scope and persistence.* They set the rules for **every** conversation, can't change mid-conversation, must handle many scenarios, and their mistakes scale to every user prompt. *"A bad system prompt is bad instructions for the whole job."* Written once, run many times — 1–3 orders of magnitude more consequential.

- **Where you touch them:** rarely. You **append** (`background.md` uses `--append-system-prompt`) or **overwrite** (Claude Code SDK, AH-3) only when building your own specialized agents. Sub-agents (`docs-scraper.md`) *are* system prompts. Only ~4 exist in the whole repo.
- **Good system-prompt sections:** Purpose (identity/role), Instructions (behavioral rules), Examples (behavior patterns), and a **loose** Workflow — because *"workflows reduce agency to increase determinism"* and a system prompt should keep agency.
- **Avoid in system prompts:** Variables, Report, Expertise/Templates, Metadata/Relevant Files/Codebase Structure.

**Retrieval:** *The tier-list grades apply to which kind of prompt?* → User prompts only.

---

## 6. The through-line: consistency is king

*"Consistency is the greatest weapon against confusion for both you and your agent."* Dan wants you **bored** of the workflow — the sameness is the feature. A predictable format lets you CRUD reusable prompts at light speed and hand work off to compute without friction. His quality test: *"If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?"*

This is how you move from inside-the-loop → outside-the-loop → **ZTE** (the TAC North Star), building AFK agents and ADW pipelines. It all traces back to one skill: **agentic prompt engineering.** *"Invest in your prompts for the trifecta to achieve asymmetric engineering in the age of agents."*

---

## 7. What "done" looks like for the student

A student has this chapter if they can, without notes: name the seven levels and the one capability each adds; state why Workflow is most-useful/mid-skill; give a real static and dynamic variable from the codebase; distinguish L6 (writes prompts) from L7 (updates its own Expertise); and explain why every grade is for user, not system, prompts — finishing by explaining why being *bored* by their own consistent format means they're doing it right.

**Next move (Dan's):** finish TAC first (ZTE/AFK/ADWs), then AH-3 (Claude Code SDK — build domain-specific agents with custom system prompts). Start at Level 1; scale to the Workflow Prompt; stack up to the Template Metaprompt.

---

*Cross-references: AH-1 (R&D framework / elite context engineering — the R and D behind prime and delegate), AH-3 (Claude Code SDK — system-prompt overwrite / domain agents), AH-4 (the O-agent — scaling parallel delegation), TAC-7 (ZTE), TAC-4 (AFK agents).*

Graded **A usefulness / S skill.** **Failure:** letting the improve step rewrite the Workflow, or building a self-improving prompt with no real domain to specialize in ("it's unlikely you even have a use case"). **Retrieval:** *What must `_improve` never touch?* → The Workflow — only the Expertise section changes.

---

## 3. The composable sections, graded (the tier list)

**Picture:** `t2740-final-tier-list.jpg` — the completed "AGENTIC PROMPT TIER LIST." This grid *is* the chapter's centerpiece. Every position below was reconciled against it.

**Sections (13), by tier:**

| Section | Useful | Skill | What it does |
|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| `## Workflow` | **S** | C | The sequential step-by-step play; maps to the agent's todo list; hosts control flow/loops/delegation. **The pillar.** |
| `## Template` | **S** | S | The exact output structure (Specified Format) with `<placeholder>` blocks; heart of L6. |
| `## Variables` | A | B | Dynamic (`$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`) + static values in `NAME: value` syntax, referenced throughout. |
| `## Examples` | A | B | Concrete output demos; can drastically raise agent performance. |
| `## Expertise` | A | A | Embedded domain knowledge; the section that makes a prompt self-improving (L7). |
| `## High Level Prompt` | B | D | Detail-void description of what you want; required core of L1. |
| `## Purpose` | B | D | 1–2 sentences of direct, agent-directed intent. |
| `## Report` | B | C | The output/format section (JSON/YAML/structure/required fields). |
| `## Instructions` | B | C | Auxiliary guardrail bullets that aid the Workflow (more valuable in system prompts). |
| `# Title` | C | D | Clear, action-oriented H1 name. |
| `## Metadata` | C | C | YAML frontmatter: allowed-tools, description, argument-hint, model. |
| `## Codebase Structure` | C | C | A *context map* (tree of where files are) — you do NOT tell the agent to read them. |
| `## Relevant Files` | C | C | A specific file set to reference; speeds the agent up. |

**Headline reading:** the most useful section (Workflow) costs only C-tier skill — high value, low cost. The peak cell (S/S) holds `## Template` and `template_metaprompt.md`.

**Two easily-confused pairs (call these out for weak students):**
- **Workflow vs Instructions** — Workflow is the *play-by-play* the agent executes; Instructions are *surrounding auxiliary notes* about the steps. You can often fold Instructions into nested Workflow bullets.
- **Codebase Structure vs Relevant Files** — Codebase Structure is a *map you do not read* (find files fast, save tokens); Relevant Files is a set you *do* read.

---

## 4. Two design frameworks to carry away

**Input → Workflow → Output.** Every prompt reads as Variables (in) → Workflow (work) → Report (out). Input and output are especially for you and your team; the workflow is where the agent does the engineering. Drop any of the three you don't need.

**Static vs dynamic variables.**
- *Dynamic* — runtime input via `$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`, changes each run. Example: `USER_PROMPT: $1` (quick-plan), `PATH_TO_PLAN: $ARGUMENTS` (build).
- *Static* — fixed value referenced throughout, changed in one place. Example: `PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: \`specs/\``. Change it to `prd/` once and every reference updates.
- Convention (from the metaprompt): dynamic variables first, static second; prefer `$1/$2` over `$ARGUMENTS` for multiple args.

---

## 5. System prompts vs user prompts

**Everything graded above is for USER prompts** — all your slash commands enter the context window as user prompts.

**System prompts are a different game** — *scope and persistence.* They set the rules for **every** conversation, can't change mid-conversation, must handle many scenarios, and their mistakes scale to every user prompt. *"A bad system prompt is bad instructions for the whole job."* Written once, run many times — 1–3 orders of magnitude more consequential.

- **Where you touch them:** rarely. You **append** (`background.md` uses `--append-system-prompt`) or **overwrite** (Claude Code SDK, AH-3) only when building your own specialized agents. Sub-agents (`docs-scraper.md`) *are* system prompts. Only ~4 exist in the whole repo.
- **Good system-prompt sections:** Purpose (identity/role), Instructions (behavioral rules), Examples (behavior patterns), and a **loose** Workflow — because *"workflows reduce agency to increase determinism"* and a system prompt should keep agency.
- **Avoid in system prompts:** Variables, Report, Expertise/Templates, Metadata/Relevant Files/Codebase Structure.

**Retrieval:** *The tier-list grades apply to which kind of prompt?* → User prompts only.

---

## 6. The through-line: consistency is king

*"Consistency is the greatest weapon against confusion for both you and your agent."* Dan wants you **bored** of the workflow — the sameness is the feature. A predictable format lets you CRUD reusable prompts at light speed and hand work off to compute without friction. His quality test: *"If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?"*

This is how you move from inside-the-loop → outside-the-loop → **ZTE** (the TAC North Star), building AFK agents and ADW pipelines. It all traces back to one skill: **agentic prompt engineering.** *"Invest in your prompts for the trifecta to achieve asymmetric engineering in the age of agents."*

---

## 7. What "done" looks like for the student

A student has this chapter if they can, without notes: name the seven levels and the one capability each adds; state why Workflow is most-useful/mid-skill; give a real static and dynamic variable from the codebase; distinguish L6 (writes prompts) from L7 (updates its own Expertise); and explain why every grade is for user, not system, prompts — finishing by explaining why being *bored* by their own consistent format means they're doing it right.

**Next move (Dan's):** finish TAC first (ZTE/AFK/ADWs), then AH-3 (Claude Code SDK — build domain-specific agents with custom system prompts). Start at Level 1; scale to the Workflow Prompt; stack up to the Template Metaprompt.

---

*Cross-references: AH-1 (R&D framework / elite context engineering — the R and D behind prime and delegate), AH-3 (Claude Code SDK — system-prompt overwrite / domain agents), AH-4 (the O-agent — scaling parallel delegation), TAC-7 (ZTE), TAC-4 (AFK agents).*

# AH-2 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of your agentic prompt engineering breaks if this nugget is missing. Tier 1 is non-negotiable; Tier 2 is the working machinery; Tier 3 is framing that keeps you consistent and honest.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering.**
Not the function, not the file — the prompt. Because each line can fire tens to hundreds of tool calls and run for minutes to hours, one great prompt buys hundreds of hours of work and one bad prompt burns them the same way. Agentic prompt engineering is now a top-tier skill, not a joke.
*Say it Dan's way:* "The prompt is now the fundamental unit of engineering. And with agents, every prompt you create becomes a force multiplier."

**2. Every prompt is built from ~13 swappable Lego-block sections — add only what you need.**
`# Title · ## High Level Prompt · ## Metadata · ## Purpose · ## Variables · ## Instructions · ## Relevant Files · ## Codebase Structure · ## Workflow · ## Expertise · ## Template · ## Examples · ## Report`. Name them whatever you want; keep the names *consistent*. Composability + consistency = reuse.
*Why weak learners lose it:* they think they must use all the sections. You don't — drop Report if you don't care about output; drop Variables if nothing comes in.

**3. The Workflow section is the pillar: most useful, only medium skill.**
Graded **S usefulness / C skill.** It's the sequential numbered play that maps straight onto the agent's todo list, and it *hosts* control flow, loops, and delegation. Master this before anything "meta."
*Test yourself:* which is more useful, `## Workflow` or `## Template`? (Both S-useful — but Template costs S-skill, Workflow only C. Workflow is the bargain.)

**4. Seven levels, each adds exactly ONE capability — reach for the lowest that works.**
1 High Level → 2 Workflow → 3 Control Flow → 4 Delegate → 5 Higher Order → 6 Template Metaprompt → 7 Self-Improving. They stack (each inherits the sections below). "Usually level three, level four is all you need." Levels 1–4 = 80–90% of real work.

**5. You're writing for the trifecta — you, your team, your agents.**
Most importantly your agents. The coworker test: *"If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?"* If yes, it's probably a high-quality prompt — and your agent will run it just as cleanly.

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery

**6. Input → Workflow → Output.** Design any prompt as Variables (in) → Workflow (work) → Report (out). Input and output are for you and your team; the workflow is for the agent. Drop any of the three you don't need.

**7. Static vs dynamic variables — one edit, everywhere.**
Dynamic = runtime input (`$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`), changes each run (`USER_PROMPT: $1`). Static = fixed value referenced throughout, changed in one place (`PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: \`specs/\``). Change `specs/` → `prd/` once and every reference follows. Convention: dynamic first, static second; prefer `$1/$2` over `$ARGUMENTS` for multiple args.

**8. Two pairs people confuse — learn the difference cold.**
- **Workflow vs Instructions:** Workflow is the play-by-play the agent *executes*; Instructions are auxiliary *notes about* the steps. Often you can fold Instructions into nested Workflow bullets.
- **Codebase Structure vs Relevant Files:** Codebase Structure is a *map you do NOT read* (find files fast, save tokens); Relevant Files is a set you *do* read.

**9. Delegation = your agent becomes the prompt engineer for its sub-agents.**
Level 4. `parallel_subagents.md` fires N stateless agents in one Task batch; the primary agent must *design self-contained prompts* with clear output expectations for each. Non-determinism is the point — five agents on five angles return five useful results. Ultra useful (S), hard to use (A-skill): you must manage information flow between agents.

**10. Control flow lives INSIDE the workflow.**
Early return: `build.md` line 17 — "If no `PATH_TO_PLAN`, STOP immediately and ask." Loop: `create_image.md`'s `<image-loop> … </image-loop>` block. Make branches/loops *visible* (numbered steps, XML delimiters) so your teammate and your agent both see where they start and stop.

**11. The peak move is a prompt that writes prompts (L6), then one that updates itself (L7).**
Template Metaprompt (`t_metaprompt_workflow.md`): a `## Specified Format` template the agent fills in — graded S/S. Self-Improving (`cc_hook_expert`): a dynamic `## Expertise` section that a *separate* `_improve` prompt rewrites — and it touches **only** the Expertise, never the Workflow.

**12. Everything in the tier list is graded for USER prompts.**
All your slash commands are user prompts (they enter the context window). System prompts are a different, higher-stakes game — see Tier 3.

---

## Tier 3 — Framing that keeps you consistent

**13. Consistency is king. Be *bored* of your own format.**

**1. The prompt is the fundamental unit of engineering.**
Not the function, not the file — the prompt. Because each line can fire tens to hundreds of tool calls and run for minutes to hours, one great prompt buys hundreds of hours of work and one bad prompt burns them the same way. Agentic prompt engineering is now a top-tier skill, not a joke.

**2. Every prompt is built from ~13 swappable Lego-block sections — add only what you need.**
`# Title · ## High Level Prompt · ## Metadata · ## Purpose · ## Variables · ## Instructions · ## Relevant Files · ## Codebase Structure · ## Workflow · ## Expertise · ## Template · ## Examples · ## Report`. Name them whatever you want; keep the names *consistent*. Composability + consistency = reuse.
*Why weak learners lose it:* they think they must use all the sections. You don't — drop Report if you don't care about output; drop Variables if nothing comes in.

**3. The Workflow section is the pillar: most useful, only medium skill.**
Graded **S usefulness / C skill.** It's the sequential numbered play that maps straight onto the agent's todo list, and it *hosts* control flow, loops, and delegation. Master this before anything "meta."

1 High Level → 2 Workflow → 3 Control Flow → 4 Delegate → 5 Higher Order → 6 Template Metaprompt → 7 Self-Improving. They stack (each inherits the sections below). "Usually level three, level four is all you need." Levels 1–4 = 80–90% of real work.

Most importantly your agents. The coworker test: *"If I handed this to a coworker, could they complete this work top to bottom?"* If yes, it's probably a high-quality prompt — and your agent will run it just as cleanly.

**6. Input → Workflow → Output.** Design any prompt as Variables (in) → Workflow (work) → Report (out). Input and output are for you and your team; the workflow is for the agent. Drop any of the three you don't need.

Dynamic = runtime input (`$1/$2/$ARGUMENTS`), changes each run (`USER_PROMPT: $1`). Static = fixed value referenced throughout, changed in one place (`PLAN_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY: \`specs/\``). # AH-2 — Outdated vs Current (mid-2026)

The **concepts** in this lesson — the trifecta, the seven levels, the composable sections, input→workflow→output, system-vs-user — have aged extremely well. What drifts is **packaging and tooling**. Treat course-era specifics as period detail; treat the tactics as current.

Rule of thumb: the tier list is timeless; the model ids and MCP dependencies are not.

---

## 1. Reusable expertise now ships as first-class **Agent Skills** (SKILL.md)

- **Course-era:** reusable prompts live as `.claude/commands/*.md` slash commands; reusable behavior lives as sub-agents in `.claude/agents/*.md`.
- **Now:** Claude Code has **Agent Skills** — `SKILL.md` with frontmatter, progressive disclosure, and on-demand discovery — as the current idiom for packaging reusable engineering so it's discoverable, composable, and shareable. The seven-levels vocabulary maps 1:1 onto a Skill body; the packaging upgraded. The Level-7 "self-improving Expertise" idea also overlaps with today's memory/knowledge-file patterns.
- **Book treatment:** teach the levels/sections exactly as filmed (they're the substance), then add a margin note: "today you'd often package a Level 2–4 workflow prompt as a Skill." Do **not** rewrite the labs onto Skills — the slash-command form is the clearest teaching vehicle.

## 2. Pinned course-era model ids (`claude-opus-4-1-20250805`)

- **Course-era:** `quick-plan.md` and `background.md` hard-code `model: claude-opus-4-1-20250805`; the README aliases and metaprompt default to generic `sonnet`/`opus`.
- **Now:** model families have moved on (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, Fable 5). The **Metadata `model:` field is exactly where you swap these.**
- **Book treatment:** annotate the two frames that show the pinned id (`t0765` quick-plan, `t2020` background) with a "period detail — pick the current best model" callout. This axis moves fastest; flag it for re-check at publish time.

## 3. Background/headless delegation → the **Claude Agent SDK** + richer headless flags

- **Course-era:** `background.md` shells out to `claude --print --append-system-prompt … --dangerously-skip-permissions --output-format text` with `run_in_background`.
- **Now:** that still works and is the clearest teaching form, but production delegation uses the **Claude Agent SDK** (Python/TS), structured `--output-format json/stream-json`, session resume, permission modes, and typed hooks — which is precisely what **AH-3 (Claude Code SDK)** builds toward. Same concept (agent as callable component; append vs overwrite system prompt), richer machinery.
- **Book treatment:** keep the CLI demo; add a forward-link box to AH-3 for "the grown-up version."

## 4. Parallel delegation → **worktree isolation** + first-class background tasks

- **Course-era:** `parallel_subagents.md` fires N `Task` sub-agents in a single batch.
- **Now:** still valid, but current practice adds **git-worktree isolation** for agents that mutate files concurrently, plus background-task orchestration and multi-agent workflow tooling. The delegation ceiling is far higher (dozens of isolated agents) than the single Task fan-out shown. **AH-4 (the O-agent)** scales exactly this.
- **Book treatment:** note the ceiling is higher than one terminal; cross-link AH-4.

## 5. Firecrawl-MCP doc scraping is **one** context-loading option

- **Course-era:** `load_ai_docs.md` depends on the Firecrawl MCP server (WebFetch fallback), with a 24-hour TTL.
- **Now:** broader native web tooling and MCP options exist; the "load docs into `ai_docs/` for agents to read" pattern is one instance of the **R&D (Reduce/Delegate)** context engineering from **AH-1**. Concept is durable; the specific MCP dependency and TTL are implementation detail.
- **Book treatment:** teach the pattern; footnote the specific MCP as swappable.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach verbatim)

- **The stakeholder trifecta** — you/your team/your agents. More true now, not less.
- **The seven levels and the ~13 composable sections** — the entire tier list. The definitive artifact of the lesson.
- **Workflow is the pillar** (S useful / C skill) — still the highest-ROI section to master.
- **Input → Workflow → Output** and **static vs dynamic variables** — pure design wisdom, tool-agnostic.
- **System vs user prompts** — scope & persistence; the framing is timeless and leads straight into agent-building.
- **Consistency is king / "be bored of your format"** — the cultural core; unchanged.
- **"Three times marks a pattern"** and the **coworker test** — durable heuristics.

---

## Overlay decision (strict: map-to-lesson / named-gap only)

Per the fan-out brief, **max 1–3** overlays with `include_in_phase1: true`. This brief supplied **no seed ID list** (unlike TAC-1), so video IDs are intentionally left `null` with `needs_id_verification: true` — Codex/Hermes must source and verify real IDs from the IndyDevDan channel before publishing links. **Do not fabricate IDs.**

| Overlay (topic) | Maps to | Phase 1? | Why |
|---|---|:--:|---|
| **Agent Skills** (Zero → Agent Skill) | corrects outdated / named gap | ✅ | Upgrades slash-command packaging to SKILL.md — the single biggest current-practice gap (§1). |
| **Claude Code SDK** (build your own agent w/ custom system prompt) | named gap / lesson's own "next lesson" pointer | ✅ | Direct continuation of the system-vs-user section; Dan explicitly forwards here (AH-3). |
| **Context Engineering** (R&D framework: priming vs memory files) | map-to-lesson (prerequisite) | ⛔ hold | Repeatedly cited (AH-1) as the basis for delegate/prime; better as a linked prerequisite than a phase-1 overlay. |

Everything else (general prompt-engineering hype, unrelated build demos) is **out** — topic drift.

1	# TAC-1 Lab Spec — Hello Agentic Coding
2	
3	**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only (`codebase/` → `tac/tac-1`; students: `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git`). No external repos, no extra dependencies beyond the lesson's prerequisite tools.
4	**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you type **zero** lines of application code by hand. Even file edits in the stretch drills go through Claude Code.
5	**Time box:** 45–75 minutes. Token cost: one interactive demo pair + 3–5 headless runs (small; but real — pay to play).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0 · Setup (10 min)
10	
11	1. Fresh directory for TAC codebases → `git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-1.git && cd tac-1`
12	2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
13	3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
14	   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
15	   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
16	   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
17	4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.
18	
19	**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.
20	
21	## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)
22	
23	**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
24	- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
25	- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.
26	
27	**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
28	- Verify all five engineering actions:
29	  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
30	  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
31	  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
32	  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
33	  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos
34	
35	**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.
36	
37	## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)
38	
39	1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
40	2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
41	3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
42	4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
43	5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
44	   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
45	   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`
46	
47	**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*
48	
49	## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)
50	
51	**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.
52	
53	**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.
54	
55	**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*
56	
57	**S4 — Map to your job (transfer).** Time drill 1A and 1B. Then write two lists from your actual work: tasks that are AI-coding-prompt-shaped vs agentic-coding-prompt-shaped. Circle the one agentic-shaped task you'd automate first with the `programmable/` pattern.
58	
59	## Pass criteria (all required)
60	
61	- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere in the lab
62	- [ ] Permissions audit answers correct (checkpoint 0)
63	- [ ] Five-action delta list correct (checkpoint 1)
64	- [ ] `demo-agentic-coding` branch exists with commit `Demo agentic coding capabilities` containing `main_aic.py` + `main_tac.py`
65	- [ ] `uv run main_tac.py` prints "hello agentic coding" + a one-line AI-agent definition
66	- [ ] All three (or four, with S2) launchers completed headlessly with a REPORT matching the real outputs
67	- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: the core four; the one-dimension delta; Claude Code's three essential elements; the contradicting truth resolved in one sentence
68	
69	## Instructor / self-check notes
70	
71	- **Most common stall:** the "new/existing branch" wording — if the branch already exists from a prior run, the agent may reuse it and the student thinks something broke. Fix: always `git branch -D demo-agentic-coding` between runs (Dan does exactly this on camera at ~17:56).
72	- **Second stall:** running the programmable script from inside the `demo-agentic-coding` branch instead of `main` — teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
73	- **Cost anxiety:** each headless run is a small number of agent turns; the lab total is modest. If a student can't run it at all, the budget conversation (pay to play) is the actual lesson surfacing early.
74	- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** skills, triggers, parallelism, CI embedding — later lessons. Deflect scope creep to keep the primitive crisp.

2. Verify the toolbelt: `claude --version`, `uv --version`, `git --version`; optional `bun --version` (TS variant). Windows: run everything inside WSL.
3. **Permissions audit (do not skip):** open `.claude/settings.json` and answer in writing:
   - Which three file tools may the agent use freely?
   - Which four git subcommands are allowed? Which git subcommands are NOT (e.g. `push`)?
   - What single non-local tool is enabled? (`WebSearch`)
4. Open the repo in your IDE, open the terminal (Cmd+J in VS Code), run `claude`.

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state, without looking, what the agent may do. If you can't, re-read the file — this habit is a graded outcome.

## 1 · Reproduce Dan — interactive A/B (15 min)

**A. Phase-1 prompt.** Copy the README **AI Coding Prompt** into Claude Code; fire.
- Verify: `main_aic.py` exists; `uv run main_aic.py` → `goodbye ai coding`.
- Note what did NOT happen: no branch, no commit, no execution by the agent.

**B. Phase-2 prompt.** Copy the README **Agentic Coding Prompt**; fire. Watch the todo checklist form, then drain.
- Verify all five engineering actions:
  1. `git branch --show-current` → `demo-agentic-coding`
  2. `main_tac.py` exists; `uv run main_tac.py` → `hello agentic coding` + one-line AI-agent definition
  3. both files were executed by the agent (outputs visible in its trace)
  4. `git log --oneline -1` → `Demo agentic coding capabilities`
  5. the agent reported what it did and cleaned up its todos

**Checkpoint 1 (write it down):** list the five actions prompt B performed that prompt A didn't. This list IS the AI-coding → agentic-coding delta.

## 2 · Reproduce Dan — programmable/headless (15 min)

1. Read `programmable/prompt.md`. Spot the two differences from the README agentic prompt *before* running anything: (a) it also CREATEs `main_aic.py` — self-contained, no dependency on drill 1; (b) it ends with a `REPORT:` block demanding the exact output of both .py files.
2. Clean slate exactly like Dan: `git checkout main && git branch -D demo-agentic-coding`
3. From a fresh terminal on `main`: `uv run python programmable/programmable.py` — hands off. No interaction allowed.
4. When it returns, verify: branch re-created, both files re-created, commit present, and the printed REPORT contains the exact outputs (cross-check by running both files yourself).
5. Run the same workflow via the other two launchers (reset the branch between runs):
   - `sh programmable/programmable.sh`
   - `bun run programmable/programmable.ts`

**Checkpoint 2:** all three launchers drove the identical workflow. Say in one sentence why the language didn't matter. *(Claude Code runs in the terminal; anything with terminal access can call `claude -p` — the agent is a function.)*

## 3 · Stretch drills (15–30 min, still zero hand-typing)

**S1 — Extend the REPORT (closed-loop thinking).** Using Claude Code (not your editor), edit `programmable/prompt.md` so REPORT also includes the current git branch name. Reset the branch; rerun the Python launcher; verify the report changed accordingly.

**S2 — Fourth launcher (prove the pattern).** Ask Claude Code to add a launcher in another language available on your machine (e.g. plain Node, Ruby, Go — anything with terminal access), following the existing three as style guides. Reset; run it; verify the identical workflow.

**S3 — Break the tool surface (permissions intuition).** Via Claude Code, remove `"Bash(git commit:*)"` from `.claude/settings.json`. Rerun the agentic prompt and observe precisely where and how the workflow halts or asks. Restore the permission. Write one sentence: what does this teach about the tools circle of the core four? *(The tool surface bounds what an agentic prompt can accomplish; permissions are part of the system design.)*

**S4 — Map to your job (transfer).** Time drill 1A and 1B. Then write two lists from your actual work: tasks that are AI-coding-prompt-shaped vs agentic-coding-prompt-shaped. Circle the one agentic-shaped task you'd automate first with the `programmable/` pattern.

## Pass criteria (all required)

- [ ] Zero application code typed by hand anywhere in the lab
- [ ] Permissions audit answers correct (checkpoint 0)
- [ ] Five-action delta list correct (checkpoint 1)
- [ ] `demo-agentic-coding` branch exists with commit `Demo agentic coding capabilities` containing `main_aic.py` + `main_tac.py`
- [ ] `uv run main_tac.py` prints "hello agentic coding" + a one-line AI-agent definition
- [ ] All three (or four, with S2) launchers completed headlessly with a REPORT matching the real outputs
- [ ] Closing oral check, no notes: the core four; the one-dimension delta; Claude Code's three essential elements; the contradicting truth resolved in one sentence

## Instructor / self-check notes

- **Most common stall:** the "new/existing branch" wording — if the branch already exists from a prior run, the agent may reuse it and the student thinks something broke. Fix: always `git branch -D demo-agentic-coding` between runs (Dan does exactly this on camera at ~17:56).
- **Second stall:** running the programmable script from inside the `demo-agentic-coding` branch instead of `main` — teaches why runbooks state their starting state.
- **Cost anxiety:** each headless run is a small number of agent turns; the lab total is modest. If a student can't run it at all, the budget conversation (pay to play) is the actual lesson surfacing early.
- **What this lab intentionally does NOT cover:** skills, triggers, parallelism, CI embedding — later lessons. Deflect scope creep to keep the primitive crisp.
